slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open with the geometric version of linear alternatives. A system is not merely feasible or infeasible in the abstract. If the target is outside a generated cone, a separating normal can prove it by being nonnegative on all generators while giving the target the wrong sign.

slides.title: Alternative Logic
slides.notes: State the alternative in a form that students can test. The primal side constructs b from the columns of A using nonnegative weights. The dual side gives a vector y that all columns accept but b rejects. The signs make mutual exclusion immediate by taking inner products.

slides.title: Cone Membership
slides.notes: Show the easy side first. When b lies in the cone, the certificate is constructive: list the nonnegative coefficients. This is the same finite-witness mentality as the previous sections, now applied to rays rather than convex combinations with weights summing to one.

slides.title: Separation Certificate
slides.notes: Now focus on the rejected target. The certificate normal gives a scalar test that every generator passes and b fails. Because nonnegative combinations preserve nonnegative pairing, the target cannot be generated. This is the cleanest way to make infeasibility visible and checkable.

slides.title: Farkas Lemma
slides.notes: Give the matrix statement after the geometry so the symbols have a job. The primal vector x is a construction certificate. The dual vector y is an exclusion certificate. Students should verify mutual exclusion by multiplying y transpose into Ax equals b and comparing the two sign conclusions.

slides.title: Strict And Weak Inequalities
slides.notes: Use this slide to slow down around inequality signs. Weak systems interact with closed cones and boundary certificates. Strict systems require positive margin or a different alternative. Homogeneous systems add scaling conventions. The lesson is practical: the certificate must match the exact system being claimed.

slides.title: Slack Variables
slides.notes: Present slack variables as translation, not as bookkeeping clutter. They turn row inequalities into an equality with nonnegative variables, exactly the setting where cone alternatives apply. The value of a slack variable also records activity, so the same device connects feasibility algebra with face geometry.

slides.title: Numerical Checker
slides.notes: Tie this slide directly to the notebook invariant. A Farkas-style certificate is a sign audit. Every generator must pair nonnegatively with the normal, while the rejected target pairs negatively. The minimum generator pairing and the target pairing are compact residuals that reveal whether the proposed certificate actually proves the alternative.

slides.title: Learner Lab
slides.notes: Use the lab to make alternatives feel testable. When the target moves inside the cone, the certificate should be nonnegative coefficients. When it moves outside, the certificate should be a separating normal. Adding a generator is a good stress test because it can invalidate a separator that previously worked.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close by returning to the two possible proofs. Either the target is constructed from the generators using nonnegative weights, or a functional separates it from every such construction. That is the practical meaning of linear inequality alternatives and the sign residuals are the quickest way to verify the claim.
